analysis.title: US Daily: Early Signs of a Tougher Labor Market for Workers Displaced from AI-Exposed Jobs
key_insights: Across nonmanufacturing industries, higher AI adoption is now associated with weaker employment growth and a higher unemployment rate, so the labor market impact of AI is broadening beyond the technology sector.

GS used the newly released Current Population Survey Displaced Worker Supplement (DWS) covering over 15,000 displaced workers who lost jobs in 2016-2025. The new data covers 2023-2025 job losses, a cohort that likely captures the first wave of AI-displaced workers.

No survey question identifies AI-caused job loss, so GS built a composite score from the occupation's AI exposure, the industry's AI adoption rate and the stated reason for separation. The score is higher when the position was eliminated.

Since 2025, workers in the top 30% of the AI displacement score took about a month longer to find a new job than other displaced workers. They were also roughly 10pp more likely to remain unemployed a year after displacement.

The short-run effects are comparable in magnitude to GS's earlier estimates for past waves of technological change. GS therefore treats those episodes as a guide to the effects of further AI-driven displacement.

In earlier technological displacement episodes, real earnings for displaced workers grew more slowly than for other displaced workers, and their probability of another unemployment spell stayed persistently higher.

In past episodes, younger, college-educated and urban workers had cumulative real earnings losses only half as large as other technology-displaced workers. Workers with shorter tenure also fared better, likely because their skills transferred more easily.

Younger AI-displaced workers took about three weeks longer than other displaced workers to return to full-time work, versus about five weeks longer for older AI-displaced workers. Younger workers also had a smaller rise in the probability of cycling through multiple jobs or holding a second job alongside the new full-time position.

GS reads the younger-worker results as a sign that younger workers may adapt more flexibly to AI disruption. This is encouraging given concerns that AI job losses could hit recent graduates hardest. College students are also shifting toward majors that feed occupations with lower AI exposure and stronger job growth.

In past technological transitions, occupational downgrading drove worse outcomes: displaced workers moved into occupations with higher routine content and lower complexity, because the same changes that eliminated their jobs eroded the value of their skills.

AI-displaced workers are significantly more likely to leave their prior occupation and industry, likely reflecting reduced demand for those jobs. On reemployment, especially older workers, they have increasingly moved into roles with similar or higher AI exposure, which leaves them vulnerable to further automation and displacement.

risk_factors: AI adoption is accelerating, and the weaker employment growth and higher unemployment tied to it now reach nonmanufacturing industries beyond technology.
AI-displaced workers re-enter roles with similar or higher AI exposure, so they face further automation and displacement risk.
Past technological displacement produced persistently slower real earnings growth and a persistently higher chance of another unemployment spell.
Recent graduates could be disproportionately affected by AI-driven job losses, though the early data on younger workers is somewhat better.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: weeks to find a new job and probability of being unemployed at the survey date, each shown as the difference between AI-displaced and other displaced workers by year. The note says there are no significant effects before 2023, and the chart marks the effect estimated during earlier waves of technological change.

Exhibit 2: cumulative real wage growth gap between technology-displaced and other displaced workers 10 years after displacement (1979-2022), split by age (under 35 vs over 35), education, geography (urban vs rural) and job tenure (under vs over 5 years).

Exhibit 3: differences between AI-displaced and other displaced workers in 2025, split by under 35 and 35 and older, for weeks to find a full-time job, probability of switching jobs multiple times and probability of holding extra jobs besides the new full-time job.

Exhibit 4: probability that a worker displaced from a job at AI risk finds a new job in an occupational category with the same or higher AI exposure risk, 2018-2025. The note says there is no change before 2023.

tension_points.bull_case: Younger AI-displaced workers are returning to full-time work faster than older ones (about three weeks longer vs about five) and are cycling through fewer temporary jobs. College students are shifting toward majors with lower AI exposure and stronger job growth.
tension_points.bear_case: AI-displaced workers take about a month longer to find jobs and are roughly 10pp more likely to be unemployed after a year. On reemployment they move into roles with similar or higher AI exposure, which leaves them open to further displacement. Past technological displacement had long-lasting earnings effects.

theme_stances.key_argument: Workers displaced from AI-exposed jobs face harder transitions back into employment and often move into roles with similar or higher AI exposure.
theme_stances.evidence: workers displaced from AI-exposed jobs face more difficult transitions back into employment
